title: Harbour Landing Homes for Sale, Regina | Prices & Listings
description: Current Harbour Landing listings, median prices, school catchments, and the honest trade-off on lot size. Regina's largest modern build-out, from an agent who sells there.
intro: Harbour Landing is the biggest planned neighbourhood Regina's built in fifty years, and almost every house in it went up after 2008. That one fact explains most of what it's like to live here. Maintenance you can predict. Modern windows. Insurance quotes that don't flinch. A street grid built around a grocery store instead of a grain elevator.

It's also the neighbourhood buyers fall for on a Saturday and second-guess by Tuesday, because the lots are small and the boulevards have no shade yet. So here's what we tell people before they write.

sections.h: What the money actually buys
sections.p: Median's around $412,000. That gets you 1,800 to 2,200 square feet, three or four bedrooms, an attached double garage, and a basement that's either finished or ready to be. Cathedral gives you more house and more land for the same money, but it comes with 1920s wiring attached. Here you're paying not to think about the house. For plenty of people that's worth it.

sections.h: Schools, and the walk to them
sections.p: Dr. George Ferguson and Harbour Landing School are both inside the neighbourhood, which is why families with young kids dominate the buyer pool. Anything within a real walking radius of either one holds its value better and sells faster in spring. One warning: the catchment boundaries cut right through the neighbourhood, so check the specific address with Regina Public Schools. Don't trust the name on the sign.

sections.h: The part that catches people out
sections.p: Lots are narrow, often 35 to 42 feet, and the houses sit close. If you want a yard your kids can play soccer in, or a garage deep enough for a truck and a workbench, you'll be happier in White City or on an older Lakeview lot. And the tree cover is twenty years out. In August this is a bright, hot, wide-open place. It isn't shady.

sections.h: Suites are worth searching for specifically
sections.p: A lot of the newer builds here were framed with a separate basement entrance, and legal suites are common enough to hunt for on purpose. A one-bedroom suite in Harbour Landing rents for roughly $1,100 to $1,250 with utilities. For a lot of buyers that's the difference between qualifying and not. Which is exactly why suited houses here go fast and almost never need a price drop.

faqs.q: Is Harbour Landing a good place to buy in Regina?
faqs.a: If you want a newer, low-maintenance house with schools and groceries you can walk to, it's probably the best choice in the city. If you want land, big trees, character or a workshop, it's the wrong neighbourhood and no amount of showings will fix that.

faqs.q: How much is a house in Harbour Landing?
faqs.a: Median sale price sits around $412,000 over a rolling year. Townhouses and condos start near $250,000. The bigger executive builds on the southern edge run into the $600,000s.

faqs.q: Are Harbour Landing homes new enough to skip an inspection?
faqs.a: No. We've found bad lot grading, failing sumps and rough basement developments in houses under ten years old. New construction changes which problems you're looking for. It doesn't remove them. Inspect anyway.

title: Cathedral Regina Homes for Sale | Character Houses & Prices
description: Cathedral listings, median prices, and a straight account of what a 1920s Regina character house really costs to own. Best value per square foot in the city, with conditions.
intro: Cathedral's the closest thing Regina has to a proper walkable neighbourhood. Elm canopy over the streets, porches people actually sit on, and 13th Avenue running the densest stretch of independent shops and restaurants in the province.
It's also where buyers most often underestimate what ownership costs. These houses are ninety-odd years old. They were built before anyone imagined a dishwasher, never mind a heat pump.

sections.h: Best value per square foot in the city
sections.p: Median's about $298,000, easily the lowest of any established Regina neighbourhood with this much going on. You typically get 1,300 to 1,700 square feet over two storeys, a 50-foot lot, and a detached garage off a paved lane. On pure dollars per foot, nothing else in Regina comes close.

sections.h: Budget for the list, then buy anyway
sections.p: Assume $15,000 to $30,000 of work on any Cathedral house that hasn't been updated recently. Panel upgrade or knob-and-tube removal, a stretch of sewer line, crack injection, shingles. We price that into every offer we write here. Counted honestly, it's still the better deal. The mistake isn't the house. It's pretending the list is empty.

sections.h: What to point the inspector at
sections.p: Three things. The electrical panel, and whether any knob-and-tube is left, because that hits your insurability before it hits your safety. The foundation, since Regina clay moves with moisture and Cathedral basements show it. And the sewer line to the street. A camera scope runs a couple hundred dollars and it's the best money you'll spend on a hundred-year-old house.

sections.h: Parking, lanes, and January
sections.p: Most houses here have no attached garage and plenty have no driveway. You park on the street or in a detached garage off the back lane, and the lanes don't get plowed on the same schedule as the streets. Two vehicles and no patience for shovelling? Think hard about that before the porch wins you over.

faqs.q: Is Cathedral a good neighbourhood in Regina?
faqs.a: For walkability, character housing and independent business it's the strongest in the city, and the best value per square foot. You trade that against old mechanical systems, street parking and small closets. People who want Cathedral tend to want Cathedral specifically, and they don't often leave.

faqs.q: How old are Cathedral houses?
faqs.a: Most were built between 1910 and 1935, with some postwar infill scattered through. Expect fir floors, plaster walls, and a basement dug for a coal furnace rather than a rec room.

faqs.q: Can you get a mortgage on an older Cathedral home?
faqs.a: Yes, but insurability drives it. The lender wants the house insured, and insurers ask about knob-and-tube, 60-amp service, oil tanks and roof age. Get an insurance quote during your condition period, not after.

title: Lakeview Regina Homes for Sale | Wascana Park Real Estate
description: Lakeview listings backing onto Wascana Park. Median prices, why inventory is so thin, and what a mid-century bungalow on a big lot is really worth in Regina.
intro: Lakeview is where Regina's mid-century professionals built, and the reason it still costs more is geography. It backs onto Wascana Park, and nobody's making any more of that edge.
Which means Lakeview rarely has much for sale, and the good ones don't sit.

sections.h: Why there's never anything on the market
sections.p: People stay here for decades. A good share of recent sales went to buyers who planned to rebuild rather than renovate. At any given moment the whole neighbourhood might have a handful of active listings. If you want in, you wait, and then you move within days when the right one shows up. That means financing sorted well in advance.

sections.h: Park proximity is the durable part
sections.p: The closer a house sits to the Wascana pathway, the better its price holds in a soft market. Backing green space, or sitting two or three doors from a pathway entrance, is the most reliable value feature in Regina residential real estate. It survives rate cycles. A renovated kitchen doesn't.

sections.h: Bungalows, rebuilds, and reading the listing carefully
sections.p: The classic Lakeview property is a 1950s or 60s bungalow on a 60 to 75 foot lot. Plenty have been taken to the studs and rebuilt behind a kept facade, clerestory windows and stone fireplace retained, everything else new. Read the remarks closely. A renovated 1962 bungalow and a studs-out 2020 rebuild are different assets at different prices, and the MLS wording doesn't always make that obvious.

sections.h: Sometimes the lot is the asset
sections.p: On the bigger Lakeview lots, especially the ones over 8,000 square feet near the park, the land carries most of the value. That should change how you read condition. A tired house on a great lot can beat a tidy one on a narrow interior lot, and we'll tell you when we think that's the case.

faqs.q: How much are homes in Lakeview, Regina?
faqs.a: Median's around $465,000 over a rolling year. Rebuilt houses and anything backing the pathway regularly clear $700,000. You can still find original-condition interior-lot bungalows in the high $300,000s.

faqs.q: Why do Lakeview homes sell so quickly?
faqs.a: Low turnover means few listings, and the group of buyers waiting for this neighbourhood is bigger than the supply. A well-priced Lakeview house often sees offers in the first week.

faqs.q: Is Lakeview good for families?
faqs.a: Yes, though the average age skews older than Harbour Landing. Park access, established schools and big lots suit families who'd rather have space and trees than a new build.

h1: The Greens on Gardiner homes for sale
title: The Greens on Gardiner Homes for Sale | East Regina Executive
description: The Greens on Gardiner listings, median prices, commute reality, and who east-end executive housing actually suits. Current inventory updated from the MLS® System.
intro: The Greens on Gardiner is Regina's east-end executive pocket. Bigger two-storeys wrapped around green corridors, quiet crescents, and a short hop onto the Ring Road.
It pulls in two kinds of buyer: people moving up from a first house, and people relocating to Regina who want something turnkey with no renovation attached.

sections.h: What the premium gets you
sections.p: Median's around $528,000, the highest of the neighbourhoods we track. That buys 2,000 to 2,600 square feet, four bedrooms, nine-foot main floor ceilings, a finished basement, and often a lot backing green space with nobody behind you. Nearly everything here went up after 2005, so triple-pane windows, an HRV and modern insulation are standard rather than upgrades.

sections.h: Pay up for the green-backing lot
sections.p: Interior lots and green-backing lots in this neighbourhood are priced closer together than they should be. A lot with no rear neighbour, facing south, holding evening sun, is a better asset than an interior lot on the same crescent. On resale it's the first thing the next buyer notices. When both are available we'll usually push you toward the green one even at a higher number.

sections.h: The commute isn't what the map says
sections.p: Google will tell you downtown is eight minutes. In a January storm with Victoria Avenue backed up, budget twenty to twenty-five. If someone in the house works at the university or downtown and hates winter driving, sit with that honestly before you fall for the crescent. The airport, on the other hand, really is quick, which is why this pocket suits people who travel for work.

sections.h: Where the market is right now
sections.p: Inventory's grown in this segment and pricing has flattened, which makes it friendlier to buyers than the $300,000 to $450,000 band. Buying here, you've got room to write conditions and negotiate. Selling here, you need to price against the last sixty days of sales, not against whatever your neighbour listed at in spring.

faqs.q: Is The Greens on Gardiner expensive?
faqs.a: It carries the highest median of Regina's major neighbourhoods at roughly $528,000, but per square foot it's competitive with newer south-end builds. You're paying for size, build year and lot quality rather than scarcity.

faqs.q: How far is The Greens from downtown Regina?
faqs.a: About 11 kilometres. Eight to ten minutes on a clear day via the Ring Road, and realistically twenty or more in winter rush hour.

faqs.q: Is now a good time to buy in the east end?
faqs.a: Inventory above $600,000 has grown and houses are taking longer to sell, which favours buyers. That's the segment where conditions and real negotiation have come back.

h1: White City & Emerald Park homes for sale
title: White City & Emerald Park Homes for Sale | Regina Commuter Belt
description: White City and Emerald Park listings east of Regina. Larger lots, no city mill rate, and an honest look at the two-vehicle cost of commuter-belt living.
intro: A quarter hour east on Highway 1 buys noticeably more house and land than the same money gets you inside Regina, with no city mill rate on top. White City and Emerald Park have absorbed a decade of families making exactly that swap.
For some households it's a great trade. For others it's quietly expensive. The deciding factor is almost never the house.

sections.h: The value case, in actual numbers
sections.p: Median's around $487,000, which out here buys 2,000 to 2,400 square feet on a quarter acre or more, often with a heated triple garage. The same lot and garage inside Regina, if you could even find it, would be well past $600,000. Taxes are lower with no city mill rate, though you'll want to confirm the current RM of Edenwold levy for the specific parcel.

sections.h: Ask about water and septic before anything else
sections.p: Don't assume services. Some properties run municipal water and sewer, some a drilled well with treatment, some a cistern with hauled water. Septic arrangements vary just as much. Each carries a different maintenance cost and a different effect on financing and insurance. Sort out which one you're buying before the offer, not during the inspection.

sections.h: The second vehicle nobody budgets for
sections.p: This is the part people miss. Out here every errand is a highway trip and almost every household runs two vehicles. Fuel, insurance, maintenance, depreciation. A good chunk of what you saved on the house goes straight back out. Families who move for the space rarely regret it. Couples who moved purely on price per square foot sometimes do.

sections.h: Schools and the bus
sections.p: White City School serves the community and older students get bussed. For young kids the ride is short and uneventful. For teenagers with activities in the city, you become the transport, most evenings, through winter. Picture that concretely before you commit.

faqs.q: Is White City cheaper than Regina?
faqs.a: Per square foot and per acre, clearly. Taxes are lower too without a city mill rate. Total cost of living is closer than the sticker price suggests once you count a second vehicle.

faqs.q: How far is White City from Regina?
faqs.a: Roughly 15 kilometres east on Highway 1. About fifteen minutes to the Ring Road, twenty to twenty-five to downtown outside of winter conditions.

faqs.q: Do White City homes have city water?
faqs.a: Many do. White City runs municipal water and sewer in the developed subdivisions. Acreage parcels outside them often rely on a well or cistern with a septic field, so always check the specific property.

title: Downtown Regina Condos for Sale | Warehouse District Lofts
description: Downtown and Warehouse District condo listings in Regina. Condo fees, reserve fund health, rental yields, and what to read before you waive your condo document condition.
intro: Downtown Regina and the Warehouse District hold the city's concrete towers and converted warehouse lofts, plus the strongest rental yields you'll find on a one-bedroom hold anywhere in Regina.
Buying a condo is a different job from buying a house. You're buying into a corporation as much as a set of rooms, and the corporation's paperwork matters more than the backsplash.

sections.h: Read the reserve fund study first
sections.p: It tells you whether the building has put away enough for the roof, the elevators, the windows and the parkade it's definitely going to need. A study that says the fund is underfunded is a special assessment waiting to land, and it'll land on you, not the seller. We read these line by line during the condo document condition. We've walked clients away from units that showed beautifully.

sections.h: What the condo fee should cover
sections.p: Downtown fees usually run $300 to $500 a month for a one or two bedroom. What matters is what's inside that number: heat, water, insurance on common property, the reserve contribution, management. A low fee isn't automatically good news. Often it means the reserve contribution is too small and you'll pay the difference later with less warning.

sections.h: The yield case, if you're investing
sections.p: A one-bedroom downtown rents somewhere around $1,250 to $1,450 against purchase prices commonly between $175,000 and $230,000. That's a better gross yield than anything in the suburbs. Net yield is what counts though, so work through the condo fee, property tax, insurance, vacancy and management. We'll build that model with you before you write.

sections.h: Concrete or wood frame
sections.p: First question to ask about any Regina condo building. Concrete means you hear the elevator and basically nothing else. Wood frame means you hear your neighbours. It shows up in resale liquidity as much as in daily comfort, and you can't tell from the listing photos.

faqs.q: Are condos a good investment in Regina?
faqs.a: Downtown one-bedrooms produce the best gross rental yields in the city. The risks are special assessments from underfunded reserves and slower resale than a house. With the documents properly reviewed they can be a solid hold.

faqs.q: What are condo fees in downtown Regina?
faqs.a: Usually $300 to $500 a month for a one or two bedroom, generally covering heat, water, common insurance, management and the reserve contribution. Get the inclusions confirmed in writing for each building.

faqs.q: What documents should I review when buying a condo?
faqs.a: Reserve fund study, the last two years of board minutes, the current budget and financials, bylaws, insurance certificate, and the estoppel certificate. The minutes tell you the most. That's where a coming assessment gets discussed first.

title: First-Time Home Buyer Regina | Programs, Costs & Listings Under $350k
description: What a first home in Regina really costs: down payment rules, no Saskatchewan land transfer tax, FHSA and Home Buyers' Plan, plus current listings under $350,000.
intro: Regina's still one of the easier places in Canada to buy a first house. Median sale price sits around $342,000, Saskatchewan charges no land transfer tax, and the entry band is properly within reach on one professional income.
The thing that stops people usually isn't the mortgage. It's the closing costs and the deposit nobody warned them about.

sections.h: What you actually need in the bank
sections.p: Minimum down payment is 5% on the first $500,000, so $17,500 on a $350,000 house. Add roughly 1.5% of the price for closing costs. Then there's the deposit, $5,000 to $10,000, payable within days of an accepted offer. That's separate money you need liquid, and it catches more first-time buyers out than anything else on this page.

sections.h: Closing here costs less than you'd think
sections.p: Saskatchewan has no land transfer tax. That one absence saves you what would be several thousand dollars in most other provinces. What you pay instead is a title registration fee tied to the value of the place, generally a few hundred dollars, plus $1,200 to $1,800 for your lawyer and a title insurance premium. Buyers moving here from Ontario or BC read that line twice.

sections.h: Open an FHSA today, before anything else
sections.p: The First Home Savings Account is the best tool a Saskatchewan first-time buyer has. $8,000 a year up to $40,000 lifetime, a deduction going in and tax-free growth coming out. It stacks with the Home Buyers' Plan, which lets you pull up to $60,000 each from an RRSP tax-free. Most people under thirty haven't opened one, and the contribution room only starts building once you do. That's the whole reason to do it now.

sections.h: What's actually in the entry band
sections.p: Under $350,000 in Regina gets you a Cathedral character two-storey, a Harbour Landing townhouse, or a two-bedroom condo downtown. Those are three different propositions once you count maintenance, monthly carrying cost and how easily you'll resell. A $268,000 townhouse with a $285 fee and a $339,000 house with a $200-a-month repair habit are closer in real cost than the prices let on.

faqs.q: How much do I need to buy a house in Regina?
faqs.a: On a $350,000 house: $17,500 for the 5% minimum down payment, about $5,000 in closing costs, and a deposit of $5,000 to $10,000 ready within days of an accepted offer. Call it $28,000 to $32,000 to be comfortable.

faqs.q: Is there a land transfer tax in Saskatchewan?
faqs.a: No. Saskatchewan charges a title registration fee based on property value instead, which on a median Regina house comes to a few hundred dollars rather than the several thousand a land transfer tax would cost you elsewhere.

faqs.q: Does a first-time buyer pay for their own agent?
faqs.a: Usually not directly. The seller's commission agreement typically covers the co-operating brokerage, so buyer representation generally costs you nothing out of pocket, and you end up with an agent who answers to you instead of to the seller.

faqs.q: What credit score do I need for a mortgage in Canada?
faqs.a: Most A-lenders want 680 or better for the best rates, and insured mortgages generally need at least 600. Below that you're into alternative lenders at higher rates. Check your score before you start shopping, not after an offer's accepted.

title: Homes with Legal Basement Suites for Sale in Regina | Mortgage Helpers
description: Regina houses with legal basement suites and secondary suites. What makes a suite legal, what it rents for, how lenders count the income, and current suited listings.
intro: A legal basement suite is what gets a lot of Regina buyers over the qualifying line, and it's one of the most searched and least understood things in this market.
The word doing all the work there is legal. A finished basement with a kitchenette isn't a suite, and no lender will treat it like one.

sections.h: What makes a suite legal here
sections.p: It has to meet the National Building Code as Regina has adopted it, and the City has to have permitted it. In practice that means a separate entrance, minimum ceiling height, egress windows in every bedroom, fire separation between units, interconnected smoke alarms, and enough ventilation and parking. Ask for the permit and the final inspection paperwork. If the seller can't produce it, treat the suite as unpermitted and price it that way.

sections.h: How lenders count the rent
sections.p: Most will use somewhere between 50% and 100% of documented suite rent toward your qualifying income, and it varies a lot between institutions. A legal, permitted, currently tenanted suite with a lease gets the best treatment. An unpermitted one often gets nothing at all. If suite income is what makes your purchase work, get the specific lender's policy in writing before you write an offer, not after.

sections.h: What a suite rents for in Regina
sections.p: A legal one-bedroom in a newer south-end neighbourhood runs roughly $1,100 to $1,250 with utilities. Two-bedrooms, and anything near the university or in Cathedral, go higher. Against a median mortgage payment that covers a serious chunk of the carrying cost, which is why suited houses draw multiple offers and rarely need a reduction.

sections.h: What you're signing up for
sections.p: You become a landlord under The Residential Tenancies Act. Rules about entry notice, deposits, rent increases, eviction. And someone else living in your building. Insurance changes too: a standard homeowner policy may not cover a rental suite, and not disclosing it can void a claim. Budget for a higher premium and actually read the policy.

faqs.q: Are basement suites legal in Regina?
faqs.a: Yes, secondary suites are allowed where they meet building code and the City has approved them. Legality comes down to separate entrance, egress windows, fire separation, alarms, ceiling height, ventilation and parking. And to the permit actually existing.

faqs.q: How much does a basement suite rent for in Regina?
faqs.a: Roughly $1,100 to $1,250 a month with utilities for a legal one-bedroom in a newer neighbourhood. Two-bedroom and university-area suites go higher.

faqs.q: Will the bank count my basement suite rent?
faqs.a: Typically 50% to 100% of documented rent from a legal permitted suite, depending on the lender. Unpermitted suites often get ignored entirely. Get your lender's policy in writing before making an offer.

faqs.q: Does a suite affect my home insurance?
faqs.a: Yes. A rented secondary suite is a material change your insurer needs to know about. A standard homeowner policy may not cover it, and not disclosing can void a claim. Expect a higher premium and get the coverage confirmed in writing.

title: Regina Investment Properties for Sale | Duplexes & Revenue Homes
description: Revenue duplexes, suited homes and investment condos in Regina. Real yield maths, financing rules for rentals, and what the numbers have to clear before we recommend a purchase.
intro: Regina throws off some of the better residential rental yields in the country, mostly because prices never ran up here the way they did in Ontario and BC while rents kept pace with everywhere else.
That doesn't make every listing a good buy. We work through the numbers first, and we say so when they don't clear.

sections.h: The numbers we work through before you write
sections.p: Price, and what the place realistically rents for in that neighbourhood, not the optimistic figure in the remarks. Then tax off the SAMA assessment, insurance quoted as a rental rather than owner-occupied, condo fee or a maintenance reserve of about 1% of value a year, vacancy at 4% to 6%, management at 8% to 10% if you're not doing it yourself, and financing at your actual approved rate. If it doesn't clear after all that, we'll tell you.

sections.h: Financing a rental is a different product
sections.p: Expect 20% down minimum on a non-owner-occupied property, since CMHC insurance isn't available for a pure rental. The rate usually sits a quarter to a half point above an owner-occupied mortgage. Lenders also apply a rental offset or add-back formula to projected income, and it varies enough between institutions to change what you qualify for. Sort the financing structure before you start shopping.

sections.h: Where the yield actually is
sections.p: Three segments, roughly in order of gross yield. Downtown one-bedroom condos, side-by-side duplexes in Cathedral and the older core, and suited single-family houses in the newer south end. The condos give the highest gross yield and the most condo-corporation risk. The duplexes give you separated mechanical systems and full control of the building. The suited houses resell best, because you can sell them to someone who wants to live there rather than only to another investor.

sections.h: Inherited tenants cut both ways
sections.p: Buying tenanted in Saskatchewan means taking on the existing tenancies under The Residential Tenancies Act, including below-market rents you can't just reset. Review the leases, rent roll, deposit ledger and payment history during your condition period. A building at gross rent well under market is only an opportunity if there's a realistic, lawful path to turnover.

faqs.q: What down payment do I need for a rental property in Canada?
faqs.a: At least 20% for a non-owner-occupied residential property. Default insurance isn't available on a pure rental, so there's no low-down-payment route. Owner-occupied properties with a suite are treated differently and can go lower.

faqs.q: What is a good rental yield in Regina?
faqs.a: Gross yields of 7% to 9% are achievable on downtown one-bedroom condos and older core duplexes. What matters is net yield after tax, insurance, reserve, vacancy and management. That's the number we model with you.

faqs.q: Can I raise the rent after buying a tenanted property?
faqs.a: Only within The Residential Tenancies Act: written notice, the required notice period, and limits on how often. You inherit the tenancy and its rent, so assume the current rent for at least a year when you're working out your numbers.

title: Acreages for Sale Near Regina | Country Properties & Shops
description: Acreages and country properties within commuting distance of Regina. Wells, septic, shops and outbuildings, acreage financing, and what to verify before you fall for the yard.
intro: An acreage inside the Regina commuter belt buys something the city can't sell you. Room. Quiet. A shop with fourteen-foot doors. A shelterbelt somebody planted forty years ago.
It also buys a set of systems that are now entirely your problem. Nobody's coming to fix your water.

sections.h: Water is the first question, not the last
sections.p: Drilled well, cistern with hauled water, or a rural pipeline. Each one has a different cost, a different reliability, and a different effect on financing. On a well, ask for a recent potability and flow test and find out the age and type of any treatment system. On a cistern, find out what hauling costs and how often. This is the thing buyers skip most often and the most expensive one to get wrong.

sections.h: Septic, and getting it inspected properly
sections.p: Most acreages run a tank with a field, a mound, or a holding tank that needs pumping. Have the system inspected specifically, because a standard home inspection usually excludes it. Ask when it was last pumped, whether it's ever backed up, and whether the field has been located and mapped. Replacing a failed field is a five-figure problem.

sections.h: Shops and outbuildings, and the appraisal gap
sections.p: A heated shop is often the real reason somebody wants an acreage, and it does carry value. But appraisers discount outbuildings harder than sellers expect, which can open a gap between the price you agreed and the value the appraisal comes back with. If a big shop is a large share of what you're paying for, plan for that gap ahead of time.

sections.h: Acreage financing is its own conversation
sections.p: Lenders treat these differently. Many will finance the house plus a limited number of acres and no more. Appraisals take longer and come back conservative. Some institutions won't lend at all without a tested potable water supply. Start with a lender who actually does acreage lending in Saskatchewan instead of assuming your existing pre-approval carries over.

faqs.q: How far out do you have to go for an acreage near Regina?
faqs.a: Most acreages within a comfortable commute sit twelve to twenty-five minutes out. Pilot Butte, White City, Balgonie, Lumsden, Pense and the surrounding RMs. Past about forty minutes the commute starts running the decision.

faqs.q: Is it harder to get a mortgage on an acreage?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Lenders often finance only the house and a limited acreage, appraise conservatively, and may require tested potable water. Use a lender experienced with Saskatchewan acreages from the start.

faqs.q: What should I check before buying an acreage?
faqs.a: Water source and its test results, septic type and condition, the age and value of outbuildings, road access and who maintains it in winter, power and gas service, and the RM's tax levy and bylaws for that parcel.
